KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Northeast winds continue to bring colder air into the region early 
this morning behind a backdoor cold front and high pressure 
building in to the north and east.

Latest model guidance holds these northeast winds for much of the 
day, setting up CAD and locking in the colder air. Temperatures
will likely be held in the 40s south of the mountains with the 
exception of southern NH and maybe the ME coast reaching the 
lower 50s late today. With the NBM having a bias of warming 
temps too quickly, have continued the trend of the last few 
forecasts in leaning much more closely on colder guidance. This 
also keeps temps in the 30s through the day in the mountains and
more on that below.

A wave of low pressure approaching from the west will result in 
precipitation overspreading the area this morning and afternoon, 
which is likely to continue into tonight. This will be just a 
cold but beneficial rain (and maybe a rumble of thunder or two
with some elevated instability) for the vast majority of NH and
western ME, but the even colder air to the north could bring a 
wintry mix today across portions of the western Maine mountains.
The result may be the first coating of snow of the season with 
guidance favoring northern Franklin over into central Somerset 
counties, although temperatures are marginal outside of the 
higher terrain in how much will stick. Forecast soundings also 
continue to indicate the possibility of sleet or freezing rain, 
but I think this would be more likely to stay in the higher 
terrain. Therefore, a winter weather advisory has not been 
issued. 

Forecast rainfall through tonight remains in the 1-1.5" for most of 
western ME and central and northern NH. Amounts taper off to 0.25" 
to 0.50" toward southern NH. 

Lastly, the HRRR does show a slightly veering of the winds and a 
downsloping signal north and west of the mountains this morning and 
afternoon, potentially resulting in gusts of 30-35 mph. 

Isolated thunder remains in the forecast for late this afternoon
and evening, especially across southern zones as instability
increase in the wake of the main stratiform precipitation shield.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

The trough exits by Wednesday morning, with subsidence and height 
rises ensuing. However a rather pronounced warm nose remains at 700 
mb. With low clouds possibly staying in the picture (especially in 
the northern highlands), unlikely we will be able to fully mix and 
erode out this stable layer aloft. In addition, soundings show 
plenty of moisture (likely enhanced from tomorrow's precipitation) 
that gets ducted/trapped below the inversion. Areas in the higher 
terrain will likely see some pockets of drizzle/fog, especially 
during the morning hours. How much clearing occurs further south is 
uncertain, but generally am cautious to accept the more bullish 
NBM/global model guidance at this point given concerns over cloud 
cover/poor mixing depth. Likely will be a raw day for interior zones 
with temps staying in the 40s again, and 50s-60s closer to the 
coast/further south. Far southern NH has the better shot at highs 
near 70 and clearing skies.

Moisture looks to finally mix out Thursday. Conditions look 
seasonable, with highs ranging from the upper 40s across the north, 
to low 60s along the coast.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...

A strengthening low pressure system will impact the Northeast U.S. 
on Friday, and keep a lingering influence on the local weather into 
the weekend. The EPS ensemble members track the low right overhead, 
while the GEFS members show a further north track, over the St. 
Lawrence River valley. Both sets of guidance show the low may deepen 
to around 990 mb, which is on the stronger side for this early in 
the cold season. The specific track will dictate if any of the 
region can get into the more mild warm sector, but in any case, 
another round of beneficial rain looks likely, with generally a half 
inch to an inch of QPF.

Very strong cold air advection by Saturday will usher in the first 
true taste of winter to the lower elevations. 850 and 700 mb 
temperatures drop below the 1st percentile on the NAEFS situational 
awareness table, which is a strong signal at this range for 
anomalously low temperatures for mid fall. Highs in the 30s in the 
interior/higher terrain appears likely, while even to the coast 
temperatures likely only reach the 40s. Lows in the 20s-30s are 
likely, possibly to the coast. Temperatures look similarly chilly 
with less wind on Sunday, before beginning to rebound early next 
week. Upslope snow showers are likely in the mountains Saturday, and 
light accumulations are possible for the higher peaks.

One other headline for the Friday-Saturday timeframe will be
